message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated that there are on the order of

\[
10^{43}\text{ – }10^{44}
\]

legal positions that can occur during a game.  This figure is often called the **Shannon number**.

More recent computational studies that count only *legal* positions (i.e., positions that could actually arise from a sequence of legal moves starting from the initial setup) give a slightly larger estimate, roughly

\[
10^{46}\text{ – }10^{47}
\]

positions.  If you include *illegal* arrangements (e.g., two kings in check, too many pawns, etc.), the count climbs to about \(10^{47}\)–\(10^{48}\).

So, in short:

| Category | Rough estimate |
|----------|----------------|
| Legal positions (reachable from the start) | ~\(10^{46}\) |
| All possible positions (legal + illegal) | ~\(10^{47}\) |
| Shannon’s original estimate | ~\(10^{43}\) |

These numbers illustrate why chess is considered one of the most complex board games in terms of combinatorial possibilities.
